[MIT](./LICENSE). That covers the studio as much as the packages, hosted or local:
anyone may run their own.


---
title: Getting started
source: apps/docs/content/docs/getting-started.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/getting-started
---

# Getting started

> Scaffold a site's configuration, connect it to the studio, publish.

## Set up a repository

```sh
npx greatcms init
```

It detects what you build with (Astro, Next.js, Nuxt or SvelteKit) and puts
content where that framework already looks for it: Astro and SvelteKit get
`src/content/cms`, the others `content/cms`.

You end up with two commented files: `.cms/schema.yaml` describing what may be
edited, and `.cms/config.yaml` describing where it goes. After asking, `init`
also adds `@greatcms/reader` to `package.json` and the one line that connects
the studio's live preview to your framework's config (the
[table on Previewing](/docs/previewing/) lists them). Each is a single additive
edit; a config it does not recognise is left alone and the line is printed for
you instead. `--no-wire` skips both. Then install with your package manager.

For a product or service business, start with the recurring pieces already
wired together:

```sh
npx greatcms init --template business
```

That gives editors company, owner/contact and search details, a hero,
reorderable page sections for features, ordered processes, statistics, stories,
products, FAQs and calls to action, and JSON collections for products and pages.
The CMS supplies the content shape; your own components still decide how every
section looks.

Render the pages collection through one dynamic route in your framework. An
editor can then add an About, Services, or legal page as a normal collection
entry; `showInNavigation` and `navigationOrder` make the menu update from the
same data. `greatcms init --template business` writes this collection for you.

## Add another kind of section

Define it and make it selectable in the page editor with one command:

```sh
npx greatcms add section testimonial --to home.sections \
  --field quote:richtext! --field name:text!
```

If the schema has only one reorderable region, `--to` is optional. Implement
the new `_type: "testimonial"` case once in your site's section renderer; from
then on editors can add, remove and reorder testimonials without touching YAML
or adding another route.

## Read a region

A region resolves to plain data. Read it through the schema-aware reader, so a
brand-new region renders its defaults before its JSON file exists. It is the
same call in every framework; only where it runs differs. In Astro, in a page's
frontmatter:

```js
import { createReader } from "@greatcms/reader";
const cms = createReader();
const hero = cms.region("home.hero");
```

In Next.js, in a Server Component, so the file is read on the server and never
fetched by the browser:

```tsx
import { createReader } from "@greatcms/reader";

export default function Home() {
  const hero = createReader().region("home.hero");
  return <h1>{hero.heading}</h1>;
}
```

In SvelteKit the same call goes in a `+page.server.js` load function, and in
Nuxt in a server route the page fetches. [The examples](/docs/examples/) run
all four.

The same reader infers types when you run `greatcms types`.

## Connect it

```sh
npx greatcms studio
```

That opens the editor for this folder in your browser, with your
dev server as the live preview beside the form: no sign-in, no settings. It
reads and writes the working copy directly, and publishing is a commit as you.
[Running the studio](/docs/running-the-studio/) covers its options, and a
studio on a server that several people and sites share.

The studio reads your schema and builds the editor from it. It never runs any
code from your repository.

## Check it

```sh
npx greatcms doctor
```

Prints every region, the file it resolves to, and which are still rendering
schema defaults.

To check the content itself: in a build, or before you push:

```sh
npx greatcms check
```

It validates every content file and collection entry against your schema, and
exits non-zero if anything would not render: a required field left empty, a
field the schema no longer has, a file no region renders, an image pointing at
something nobody committed. `--json` reports the same to a machine.

A region with no content file is not a failure: it renders schema defaults,
which is the point.


---
title: The command line
source: apps/docs/content/docs/the-command-line.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/the-command-line
---

# The command line

> Scaffold, extend, type, check, and inspect a site from the terminal.

Everything the CLI does runs on your machine with your toolchain. It edits the
two files in `.cms/`, reads your content, and never talks to a studio. One
command, `greatcms studio`, runs one: on this machine, for this folder.

`greatcms help <command>` (or `greatcms <command> --help`) shows a command's
options and examples, and `greatcms --version` prints the version. Short flags
work where they exist (`-y` for `--yes`, `-f` for `--force`, `-o` for `--out`),
`--` ends the options, and a misspelt command or option gets a suggestion
rather than silence. `--no-color` or `NO_COLOR=1` gives plain text.

When a newer release is on npm, a command run in a terminal says so on its last
line, with the command that updates the project. npm is asked at most once a
day, with a short time limit, and never from a script or CI;
`GREATCMS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` turns it off.

The exit status is meant for scripts: `0` when done, `1` when the command failed
or found problems (such as `check` finding content that will not render), `2`
when it was called wrongly, and `130` when you cancelled a prompt.

## Tab completion

`greatcms completion <shell>` prints a completion script for bash, zsh or fish,
covering commands, options, and the values they take:

```sh
greatcms completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/greatcms
greatcms completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_greatcms"
greatcms completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/greatcms.fish
```

## `greatcms init`

```sh
npx greatcms init
```

Detects the framework (Astro, Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit, or nothing in
particular), puts content where that generator already looks for it, writes a
commented `.cms/schema.yaml` and `.cms/config.yaml` with the editor's `$schema`
line for autocomplete, and prints the snippet that reads your first region in
your framework's own syntax.

Templates: `hero` (one region), `landing` (a page of reorderable blocks),
`business` (a complete small-business content model), `blog`, and `blank`.
It also adds `@greatcms/reader` to `package.json` and connects the studio's
live preview in your framework's config: one additive line each, shown before
anything is written. A config it does not recognise is left alone and the line
is printed instead; `--no-wire` skips this step entirely.

`--yes` takes every default, and `--framework`, `--template`, `--name`, and
`--dir` override one answer each, so it scripts as well as it prompts. It
refuses to overwrite an existing setup without `--force`.

## `greatcms setup`

```sh
npx greatcms setup ./my-project
```

The guided version. It scans the target directory, detects the framework and
package manager, and finds child projects as well as apps under `apps/`,
`packages/`, and `examples/`. Choose a discovered app or the folder itself, then
either start from a template or build a content model field by field: regions,
reusable sections, reorderable page sections, collections, and groups for
related details such as an owner or opening hours.

Every planned file is shown before anything is written, and cancelling writes
nothing. The scan reads configuration data only. It does not execute project
code, follow symbolic links, or look inside dependencies.

## `greatcms add`

The second managed section is the one that used to mean hand-editing YAML.

```sh
npx greatcms add region about.intro --field heading:text! --field body:richtext
npx greatcms add section testimonial --to home.sections --field quote:richtext! --field name:text!
npx greatcms add block card --field title:text! --field body:text
npx greatcms add collection guides --format mdx --field content:richtext
```

A field is `name:type`, with a trailing `!` for required. Types are `text`,
`richtext`, `image`, `link`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `file`, `select(a|b)`,
`list(text)`, and `blocks(card|grid)` for a nested list. `add section` defines a
block and adds it to a reorderable region's allow list in one edit; when the
schema has only one such region, `--to` is optional.

The schema is edited **as text**, so the comments explaining your site's own
decisions survive. It refuses rather than corrupts: a duplicate name, an id the
standard would reject, or a nested block that does not exist all stop before
the file changes. Run it with no fields in a terminal and it asks.

## `greatcms types`

```sh
npx greatcms types --out src/cms.d.ts
```

An interface for every region, block, and collection, with select options as
unions and blocks discriminated by `_type`, plus a module augmentation that
types the reader by id. `cms.region("home.heroo")` becomes a compile error. A
field with a `default` is non-optional, because resolution guarantees it a
value.

`--check` exits non-zero when the committed file no longer matches the schema,
which is how CI notices a schema change nobody regenerated the types for. A
site that never runs it loses nothing: without the file, the reader takes any
string.

## `greatcms check`

```sh
npx greatcms check
# content: OK (3 regions, 6 entries, 1 media reference, 4 internal links)
```

Validates every content file and collection entry against the schema and exits
non-zero if anything would not render, or would render broken:

- a required field left empty, a field the schema no longer has, a file no
  region renders any more, frontmatter that will not parse;
- an image or file pointing at an upload nobody committed, whether it sits in
  an image field, a link, a rich-text `<img>`, or a Markdown `![]()`;
- an internal link to an entry that does not exist;
- a `pattern` that could not be checked within a tenth of a second
  (`pattern_timeout`), so one that backtracks without end fails the build
  instead of hanging it.

Each report names the file, the field path, and what to do.

Internal links are link fields, rich-text `<a href>`, and Markdown links whose
target starts with `/`. `check` drops the `#fragment`, the `?query`, a trailing
`.html` and a trailing slash, then reads the path back through
`preview.paths` in `.cms/config.yaml`: with `updates: "/updates/{slug}"`,
`/updates/launch` is broken unless `content/updates/launch.md` exists, and with
`pages: { home: "/", "*": "/{slug}" }`, `/` needs a `home` page. A path that
matches no pattern, like `/assets/report.pdf`, is a route the site writes
itself and is left alone, as is the index a pattern sits under (`/updates`).
Without `preview.paths`, links are counted but not checked.

Some things are worth fixing but never break a build. `check` reports them as
warnings, lists them apart from problems, and still exits zero:

- an upload in `content.media` that no region, entry, unpublished draft or
  schema default refers to (dotfiles such as `.gitkeep` are ignored). `check`
  only reads content, so a file the site's own code imports shows up here too;
- a rich-text link with no text, which a screen reader announces as its URL;
- headings in one rich-text field that skip a level, such as `h2` then `h4`.

`--json` gives the same report to a machine: `ok` is false only when `issues`
is non-empty, and warnings come in their own `warnings` array.

A region with no content file is never a failure. It renders schema defaults,
and `check` says so.

## `greatcms doctor`

Prints every region, the file it resolves to, which ones are still rendering
schema defaults, and any unsaved edit left in `.cms/draft/`: the one thing that
shows in your dev server and nowhere else.

It also names any source file that fetches fonts from another site while the
page loads (Google Fonts and the like), which is what makes text move when
they arrive, and says how to serve them from the site instead. It is a
warning, not a failure.

## `greatcms fonts`

For an Astro site that loads Google Fonts. It reads the font link the site
already has and makes the change itself: each family goes into `astro.config`
under `fonts`, a `<Font>` tag for it into the layout's head, the CSS points at
the new variables, and the old link, `@import` and preconnects are removed.
The fonts are then served by the site, with fallbacks sized to match and no
swap after first paint, so text does not move.

```sh
greatcms fonts --dry-run   # say what would change, write nothing
greatcms fonts             # make the change; review it with git diff
```

It plans every edit before making any. If the config already sets fonts, a
font is loaded in a way it does not recognise, or the site is not on Astro 6
or newer, it changes nothing and says why. Run it once per site, and again
only when the site adds a typeface.

## `greatcms studio`

```sh
npx greatcms studio
```

Opens the visual editor for the site in this folder, or the nearest folder
above it with a `.cms/schema.yaml`: the studio on `127.0.0.1:4983`, your
browser opened on it with no sign-in, and the site's dev server
as the live preview. `--port`, `--dev-url`, `--no-dev` and `--no-open` change
the defaults; [Running the studio](/docs/running-the-studio/#on-your-own-machine)
has the details. The dev server is started by this command, as your own dev
script would be; the studio still runs nothing from the repository.

## `greatcms describe`

The content model in one screen, for whoever is about to write content by
hand: a person, or a coding agent. Every region with its file, every block
with its variants, every collection with its entry path, the slugs that exist
and the page each becomes; and each field as one line with its type, limits,
condition, default and the schema's own description:

```
region home.hero → content/cms/home.hero.json
  eyebrow: text (≤ 60 chars)
  lines: list<text> (1–4 items)  # The headline, one line per item
  primary!: link
block selected-work  _variant: grid | stacked (first is the default)
  heading!: text (≤ 60 chars)
collection work → content/work/<slug>.json  page /work/{slug}/
  entries: atlas-rail, fernhouse, lumen, oculi, tidewater
```

`!` marks a required field. `--json` gives the same outline as data.


---
title: The hybrid model
source: apps/docs/content/docs/the-hybrid-model.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/the-hybrid-model
---

# The hybrid model

> Why a region is opt-in, and what happens before anyone edits anything.

Most of a page is code. A headline, a pricing table, and a rotating set of
feature cards are not: those change on a marketing schedule rather than a
release schedule, and they are the reason people install a CMS at all.

GreatCMS manages only what you list. Everything else is ordinary code the studio
never sees, never parses, and cannot break.

## Regions

A **region** is a named slice of a page: `home.hero`, `pricing.faq`. The id
doubles as the file name, so `home.hero` is stored at
`<regions dir>/home.hero.json`.

A **blocks region** holds an ordered list an editor can add to and reorder, from
a set of block types you allow. A **collection** is a folder of entries sharing
a shape, a blog, case studies, a changelog, stored as Markdown with
frontmatter, which is what every static site generator already expects.

## Defaults are not a fallback, they are the starting state

A missing content file is never an error. The region resolves to the `default`
values declared in the schema, so a site is correct **before the CMS has ever
run**, and stays correct if a field is added to the schema before anyone edits
it.

Stored content layers over those defaults: objects merge deeply, arrays are
replaced wholesale, and each block in a list is merged over its block type's
own defaults.

## What a site depends on

Its own files. There is no network call, no database, and no API key in a build.
The schema is part of the site and is committed alongside the code. What a site
never depends on is the studio: shut it down permanently and every site it
managed keeps building.


---
title: Publishing
source: apps/docs/content/docs/publishing.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/publishing
---

# Publishing

> One commit in your working copy, or nothing at all.

A site is a folder on the machine the studio runs on. Publishing writes the
content files into that folder and commits them on whatever branch is checked
out. The commit is the deploy trigger: push it, and whatever CI the repository
already had does the rest. There is no webhook to configure and no cache to
purge.

A folder that is not a Git repository works too. The files are written, and
that is the whole job.

## One commit, or none

A publish touching a region and three uploaded images is **one commit**. Every
file is written to a temporary file first and then moved into place, so a full
disk or a bad path fails before any real file has changed. If Git refuses the
commit (a held `index.lock`, a missing `user.email`, a path in `.gitignore`), the
editor says so instead of reporting a publish that never happened.

Publishes to the same folder run one at a time, so a double-click or two open
tabs cannot interleave their writes.

The studio never runs your repository's Git hooks. They are code in the
repository, and the studio does not execute anything from a repository it
manages. Checks belong in CI, where they run on every commit anyway.

## Pushing for you

For an editor who should never see Git, turn on **Push after every publish**
in the site's settings. Each publish is then pushed to the branch's upstream,
and the host deploys it the way it deploys any push: edit, publish, live.

The push uses the Git credentials of the machine the studio runs on, never
prompts for a password, and never runs a pre-push hook. If it fails, the
commit is still there and the editor is told it is not live yet, with the
reason: most often the remote has commits this copy lacks, which
`git pull --rebase` in the site's folder sorts out. Publishes waiting to go
out are listed on the site's page, with a **Push now** button.

## Conflicts

A publish carries the commit the editor started from. If the content being
published changed since then, in a newer commit or as an uncommitted edit
someone made by hand, the publish is refused rather than overwriting it. Reload,
then publish again. A commit that touched other files is not a conflict, so
working on the site's code does not interrupt anyone editing its content.

Creating an entry never replaces one: if the title would produce a file name
that already exists, the studio asks for a different one.

## Validation happens first

Content is checked against the schema before anything is written, so invalid
content never reaches the repository. Alt text is part of that: the only way to
store an empty one is a field explicitly marked `alt: decorative-allowed`.

Run `greatcms check` in CI to hold hand-edited content to the same rules.


---
title: Managing content
source: apps/docs/content/docs/managing-content.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/managing-content
---

# Managing content

> A site's owner and editors, day to day in the studio, and what each button becomes in Git.

The studio is where the people who look after a site change its words and
images without opening a code editor or a terminal. Everything it does ends as
files in the site's repository, so this page follows a day's work from the
screen to the commit. Installing it is covered in
[Running the studio](/docs/running-the-studio/).

## Connecting a site

On your own machine `npx greatcms studio`, run in the site's folder, opens the
studio with that site already connected. On a shared studio, connecting is the
owner's job, done once per site from **Connect a site**:

- **From GitHub.** The repositories you gave the studio on GitHub are
  listed, those already using GreatCMS first. Tick any number and press
  **Add selected**: one with a schema opens as a site, any other waits for a
  starter.
- **In the sites folder.** Folders in the studio's sites folder are listed;
  one with a schema connects with a click.
- **Copy from Git.** Paste any https or SSH address. Only files are fetched:
  no hooks, no submodules.
- **By path.** Any other folder on the machine.

A folder with no `.cms/schema.yaml` offers **Set up**: choose one of the
`greatcms init` starters, and the studio commits `.cms/schema.yaml` and
`.cms/config.yaml` in one commit and connects the site, changing nothing else.
The variables behind each way are in
[Connecting a site](/docs/running-the-studio/#connecting-a-site).

## A site at a glance

![The Paraline site in the studio: its working copy, a running live preview, publishing as one commit, and cards for each page region and collection with who edited it last.](/screens/studio-site.webp)

A site's page is where editors start. It says where the working copy is,
whether the live preview is running, and where a publish goes: one commit, or
one commit pushed to the branch's upstream. Below that, every **page region**
(one part of the site, such as the home page's hero) and every **collection**
(a list of entries, such as projects or posts) is a card saying who changed it
last. Further down are recent changes from Git, unsaved edits nobody has
published, publishes scheduled for later and, on a server with the builder,
what is live.

The sidebar holds the same list, plus **Search content**, which finds words in
every region and entry, unpublished drafts included, and opens the field that
holds them. Press `/` to jump to it.

## Editing a region or an entry

The form is built from the site's schema: one control per field, labelled and
described the way the schema describes it, with the limits it sets. A list
grows by filling its empty row. An image takes an upload or one already on the
site, and will not save without alt text unless the field allows an empty one.
A field of sections offers **Add a section**, with arrows to reorder and
**Remove** on each one.

Every one of those actions is an ordinary form post. With JavaScript switched
off the editor still adds, reorders and publishes; the script only makes it
quicker. Content is checked against the schema before anything is written, and
a field that fails says why beside it.

Entries in a collection are added from the collection's page, or the **Add**
link on its card, and each entry's file name comes from the field the schema
names, usually its title. Creating one never
replaces another: if the name is taken, the studio asks for a different title.

## The visual editor

![Editing the body of a project in the visual editor: bold, italic, two heading levels, paragraph, lists, quote, code and link in the toolbar, and the new paragraph already on the page in the live preview beside it.](/screens/studio-richtext.webp)

A rich-text field opens in a visual editor built on ProseMirror: bold, italic,
two heading levels, paragraphs, bulleted and numbered lists, quotes, code and
links, with `Ctrl` or `Cmd` and `B`, `I` and `Z` doing what they usually do. It
deliberately stops there: this edits web copy, and the site's own design does
the rest.

What it stores is plain HTML, so any language can render it without a library.
Underneath it is a real textarea holding that HTML, and the form submits the
textarea. If the editor's script is blocked or fails, the textarea is simply
shown and editing carries on. Only screens with a rich-text field load the
script at all.

The body of an MDX entry is code the site's build runs, so only the owner
changes it; an editor sees it and cannot alter it. See
[People](/docs/running-the-studio/#people).

## The live preview

![The Home hero region with Select switched on: the third headline line changed to "move" in the form already reads that way in the preview, and pointing at the paragraph under the headline outlines it with its field name, Lede.](/screens/studio-region.webp)

When a site has a dev server, the editor frames it beside the form. It is the
real site, rendered by its own components, not an imitation of it. As you type,
each change is written to `.cms/draft/` in the working copy a moment later, the
dev server reloads, and the page shows content nobody has published. Drafts
never reach a build, and publishing clears them.

The buttons above the frame:

- **Select** turns the page into a map of the form. Point at a heading,
  paragraph or image and it is outlined with its field's name; click it and that
  field opens in the form, focused. Going the other way, landing in a field
  scrolls the page to where it renders.
- **Sections** outlines every section on the page at once.
- **Desktop** and **phone** width, **reload**, **open in a new tab**, and
  **share a preview link**, which anyone can open for seven days without an
  account (see [Sharing the preview](/docs/self-hosting/#sharing-the-preview)).

Leave the editor with unpublished edits and they are still there when you come
back, with a notice saying so. **Discard unsaved edits** throws them away and
puts the preview back to what is published. More on this, including how to
point the inspector at a value the site transforms, in
[Previewing](/docs/previewing/).

## Publishing

**Publish** writes everything in the form, and any images it uploaded, as one
commit in the site's working copy, or nothing at all if anything fails. An
editor's publish is committed under their own name and email, so `git log`
says who changed what. `Ctrl` or `Cmd` with `Enter` does the same.

If the same content was published by someone else since you opened it, your
publish is refused rather than overwriting theirs. **Publish later** keeps the
form as it is and publishes it at the time you choose, through the same path;
the site's page lists what is waiting and lets you cancel it.

With **Push after every publish** on in the site's settings, each commit is
pushed to the branch's upstream, and the host deploys it as it deploys any
push. Details, and what happens when a push fails, are in
[Publishing](/docs/publishing/).

## History and rollback

Every region and entry has a **History** link listing the commits that changed
it, with the author, the date and the commit. **Restore this version** opens that version
in the editor as an unsaved edit: it shows in the preview first, and publishing
it makes one new commit. Nothing in Git is rewritten.

On a server where the builder deploys the site, the site's page also shows what
is live, any build that failed with its log, and the releases kept on disk.
**Put this back live** returns the site to one of them until the next publish;
see [The builder](/docs/self-hosting/#the-builder).

## People

The owner signs in with the studio password and is the only one who connects
sites, changes their settings and manages people. From **Editors** the owner
adds each person with a name, an email and a password of their own, and ticks
the sites that person may open. Editors change content: regions, entries,
images, drafts and publishes. When two people have the same content open, each
sees the other's name.

With GitHub connected, **Continue with GitHub** is the sign-in, and a password
is a link away. Whoever can
push to a site's repository on GitHub edits that site here, and sees only that
site. Give or remove access on GitHub: nothing is set up in the studio.

Form submissions from the site land in the **Inbox**, separate from content;
see [Forms and submissions](/docs/forms-and-submissions/).

## Branches and review on GitHub

By default a publish lands on the branch the working copy has checked out. To
keep publishes off the live site until someone has looked at them, type a new
name into **Branch** in the site's settings. The studio starts that branch from
the current one, or picks it up from the remote if it is already there, and
every publish is committed on it and, with pushing on, pushed to the branch of
the same name.

When the remote is on GitHub, the site's page then links **Review and merge on
GitHub**, the comparison between that branch and the repository's main one.
Review, comment and merge there, and the host deploys the merge. Switching
branches is refused while the folder has changes that are not committed, so
nobody's work is carried across by accident.

## Git access

**Git access** is where the owner lets the studio reach repositories it does
not already have credentials for.

- **GitHub.** The studio creates its own GitHub App in two clicks, and you
  choose which repositories it may use. Each copy and each push gets a token
  that lasts an hour, passed only to that one Git command, so no credential is
  written into a repository or onto a command line.
- **Other hosts.** For GitLab, Bitbucket or your own server, save an access
  token for the host. It is kept in Git's own credential store and used for
  copying and for pushing after a publish alike.

Whichever way a repository arrives, the studio never runs anything from it:
not a build, not a hook. Previews are the site's own dev server, and checks
belong in CI.


---
title: Running the studio
source: apps/docs/content/docs/running-the-studio.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/running-the-studio
---

# Running the studio

> One process, one SQLite file, one password. Nothing it manages depends on it.

The studio is a single Node process. It keeps its own state, the list of sites
and the submissions inbox, in one SQLite file, and reads and writes the sites it
manages as folders on the same machine. Hosted or local, it is open source
under the MIT licence, and anyone may run their own.

## On your own machine

In a site's folder, one command opens the editor for it:

```sh
npx greatcms studio
```

It starts the studio on `127.0.0.1:4983`, or the next free port, with this
folder as its one site, and opens it in your browser with no sign-in. The
live preview is the site's dev server: the one already running, or your own
dev command, started here and stopped with it.
Publishing commits to the working copy as you; nothing is pushed. This
studio is for that one project: it has no list of sites, nothing to connect
or disconnect, and no editors to add.

It trusts whoever can reach it on this machine, other users of a shared one
included, which is why it only listens on loopback. `--host` with any other
address is refused unless `STUDIO_PASSWORD` is set, and then you sign in
with that instead.

| Option            | Meaning                                              |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `--port <number>` | The studio's port, exactly; an error if it is taken. |
| `--dev-url <url>` | Use this dev server and start none.                  |
| `--no-dev`        | Edit without a preview.                              |
| `--no-open`       | Print the address without opening a browser.         |

It needs Node.js 22.13 or newer and the `@greatcms/studio` package, which the
command offers to add to the site the first time, showing the exact install
command and asking before it runs. Its database and session secret go in
`node_modules/.cache/greatcms`, or your user cache folder when the site has no
`node_modules`: never in a file Git tracks. Ctrl+C stops everything.

## On a server

```sh
STUDIO_PASSWORD='something long' pnpm --filter @greatcms/studio start
# GreatCMS studio on http://localhost:8787
```

Or as a container, from the published image. Mount the folder that holds your
sites, since the studio edits them in place, and a volume for its database:

```sh
docker run -p 8787:8787 -e STUDIO_PASSWORD='something long' \
  -v greatcms-data:/data -v ~/sites:/sites \
  ghcr.io/uwenayoallain/greatcms-studio
```

Then connect `/sites/my-site` in the studio. `apps/studio/Dockerfile` builds
the same image from a checkout. `STUDIO_PASSWORD` is required and deliberately
has no default.
For a server that also builds and serves the site, see
[Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/).

## Environment

| Variable                 | Meaning                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `STUDIO_PASSWORD`        | Required. Changing it signs every open session out.                                                              |
| `STUDIO_SECRET`          | Signs session cookies. Generated on start if unset, which means sessions reset on restart.                       |
| `STUDIO_DB`              | Path to the SQLite file. Defaults to `data/studio.sqlite`.                                                       |
| `PORT`                   | Defaults to `8787`.                                                                                              |
| `STUDIO_SITES`           | Sites to manage from the first start, as JSON; see [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/).                          |
| `STUDIO_URL`             | Where browsers reach the studio, so a proxy's `forward_auth` can send visitors here to sign in.                  |
| `STUDIO_COOKIE_DOMAIN`   | Parent domain the preview's sign-in cookie covers, e.g. for `preview.`; see [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/). |
| `STUDIO_TRUST_PROXY`     | `1` behind a reverse proxy you control, `cloudflare` behind Cloudflare. Unset when reachable directly.           |
| `RESEND_API_KEY`         | With `NOTIFY_FROM` and `NOTIFY_TO`, emails each form submission. Without them, submissions are only stored.      |
| `STUDIO_WEBHOOK_URL`     | Posts every submission and every publish as JSON to this `http(s)` URL. Slack and Discord webhooks work as is.   |
| `STUDIO_SUBMISSION_DAYS` | Deletes submissions older than this many days. Unset: they are kept.                                             |
| `STUDIO_TIMEZONE`        | The zone times are shown in and "Publish later" is typed in, e.g. `Africa/Kigali`. Defaults to the server's.     |
| `STUDIO_LOCALE`          | The language tag dates and times are written in, e.g. `en-GB` or `fr`. Defaults to `en`.                         |
| `STUDIO_OWNER_NAME`      | What others see the password's owner called. Defaults to `Owner`.                                                |
| `STUDIO_SITES_ROOT`      | The folder of sites the connect page lists, and where copies go.                                                 |
| `STUDIO_CLONE_PRIVATE`   | `1` lets Copy from Git reach this machine and its private network, for a Git server that lives there.            |
| `STUDIO_GITHUB_OWNERS`   | GitHub logins, comma-separated, that are owners when they sign in. Unset: the person who owns the GitHub App.    |
| `STUDIO_GITHUB_URL`      | A GitHub Enterprise Server address, when that is your GitHub. Defaults to `https://github.com`.                  |

Behind a proxy, `STUDIO_TRUST_PROXY` lets rate limiting see the visitor's
address rather than the proxy's, and marks the session cookie `Secure`. The
studio uses the last `X-Forwarded-For` entry, the one your proxy appended, or
`CF-Connecting-IP` for Cloudflare. Leave it unset when the studio is reachable
directly: those headers are then the visitor's to forge.

## Connecting a site

A site is a folder on the machine the studio runs on. **Connect a site** finds
one three ways:

- **From GitHub.** Connect GitHub once: the studio makes its own GitHub App
  and you choose the repositories it may use. They are listed with the ones
  that already use GreatCMS first; tick any number and **Add selected**
  copies each, signing in with a token that lasts an hour. One with a schema
  is connected as it lands; any other offers **Set up**.
- **In the sites folder.** With `STUDIO_SITES_ROOT` set, the page lists the
  folders in it. One with a schema connects with a click, named after its
  folder; one without offers **Set up**.
- **Copy from Git.** Paste any https or SSH address, without a token in it:
  for a private repository, save one on **Git access**. Only files are
  fetched: no hooks, submodules or redirects. The host is looked up once and
  the copy held to that address, so a name cannot answer differently the second
  time. Two copies run at a time, each up to 2 GB, made beside the database
  where no site's code can write and moved into the sites folder when whole.
- **By path.** Any other folder; `~` is the studio user's home.

The studio reads `.cms/schema.yaml` from that working copy and builds the
editor from it. There is no token and no network call. Give it your dev
server's URL and the editor frames your real site beside the form; see
[Previewing](/docs/previewing/). With `STUDIO_PREVIEW_URL` set, a site
connected without one gets its own; see [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/).

A folder with no schema gets **Set up**: pick a `greatcms init` starter, and
the studio commits `.cms/schema.yaml` and `.cms/config.yaml` and connects the
site, changing nothing else.

A new **Branch** in a site's settings keeps publishes off the live one, to
review and merge on GitHub.

## People

The owner signs in with `STUDIO_PASSWORD` and leaves the email empty. From
**Editors** in the sidebar the owner adds people by name, email and a password
of at least twelve characters. Each signs in as themselves, and each publish
is committed under their name and address, so `git log` says who changed what.
An editor opens only the sites the owner ticks for them there, or every site
if that box is ticked; one added before this choice existed keeps every site.

Sites and people stay the owner's: an editor cannot connect, reconfigure or
disconnect a site, or manage editors, and reads an MDX entry's body without
changing it, because MDX is code the site's build runs. Removing someone signs
them out on their next request. Two people with the same content open see each
other's name; if both publish, the second is refused, not overwritten.

### Sign in with GitHub

A new studio is opened once with `STUDIO_PASSWORD`, which leads straight to
connecting GitHub. From then on the sign-in page is **Continue with GitHub**,
with the password behind a link for the owner and for editors given one.
Whoever GitHub lets push to a connected site's
repository edits that site and sees no other: its content, images, history,
search and inbox.

- The studio asks GitHub who may push, believes the answer for under two
  minutes, and asks again on every publish. Access removed on GitHub ends here.
- It asks for no email and keeps no token. Commits are authored as
  `id+login@users.noreply.github.com`.
- Signing in never connects a repository. Someone who can push to none of the
  connected sites sees a page saying so.
- The person who owns the GitHub App is an owner; `STUDIO_GITHUB_OWNERS` names
  others instead. Disconnecting GitHub signs all of them out.

Search, history, scheduled publishes and the rest of a day's editing are in
[Managing content](/docs/managing-content/).

## What it will not do

The studio never executes anything from a repository it manages: not a build,
not a Git hook, not a schema that happens to be code. Schemas are data. A
preview is your own dev server. Checks belong in CI, where they run on every
commit anyway.

Shut the studio down and every site it managed keeps building from what is in
Git. That is the point of the whole arrangement, and it is why one studio can
manage several sites without carrying a toolchain for each.

## Security headers and rate limits

Every response carries a strict `Content-Security-Policy`, and a preview URL
the browser would execute (`javascript:`, `data:`) is refused. Sign-in attempts
and form intake are rate limited per address, and uploads are checked by their
bytes rather than their extension: an SVG, which can carry script, is refused as
an image.


---
title: Self-hosting
source: apps/docs/content/docs/self-hosting.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/self-hosting
---

# Self-hosting

> One server, three containers; an editor publishes and the site is live in seconds.

Nothing here needs a platform. A site built with GreatCMS is files, so the whole
of it, editing included, fits on one small server:

- **The studio**, where editors sign in and publish. Each publish is a commit in
  the site's working copy on that server.
- **The builder**, `greatcms-deploy`, which watches that working copy, builds
  every new commit in a clean checkout, and swaps the live folder when the build
  succeeds. A failed build changes nothing; the previous release stays up.
- **A web server** serving the live folder, with the studio behind the same
  reverse proxy. Caddy gets HTTPS for free.

Editors never touch Git, a terminal, or a dashboard. Publish, wait a few
seconds, reload.

## The builder

```sh
DEPLOY_SOURCE=/srv/sites/my-site DEPLOY_ROOT=/srv/www npx greatcms-deploy
```

It checks the branch tip every few seconds. For a commit that is not live it
clones the repository into a work folder, runs the build command (by default
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build`), moves the output into
`releases/<sha>`, and repoints the `current` symlink in one rename. Serve
`DEPLOY_ROOT/current` and a visitor always sees a whole release, never a
half-written one. The last few releases are kept so you can roll back by moving
the symlink.

| Variable          | Meaning                                                         |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEPLOY_SOURCE`   | The repository: a path on the server, or any URL git can clone. |
| `DEPLOY_ROOT`     | Holds `releases/`, `current` and `status.json`.                 |
| `DEPLOY_BUILD`    | The build command. Runs in the checkout with `CI=1`.            |
| `DEPLOY_OUTPUT`   | The folder the build writes, relative to the checkout. `dist`.  |
| `DEPLOY_BRANCH`   | `main`.                                                         |
| `DEPLOY_INTERVAL` | Seconds between checks. `10`.                                   |
| `DEPLOY_KEEP`     | Releases kept for rollback. `5`.                                |

`status.json` records what is live and, until a later commit builds, the newest
one that failed with the tail of its build log. `greatcms-deploy status` prints
it; `greatcms-deploy once` builds and exits, for a cron job or a CI step.

## What runs a site's code

The builder and the preview service run the site's build, its dev server and
its packages' install scripts; the studio
[runs none of it](/docs/running-the-studio/). Both compose files give each a
container and a network of its own, out of reach of the studio and the tunnel,
and every container a read-only root, no capabilities, and memory and process
limits. `docker compose up -d` alone restores a stopped stack. What that costs:

- Dev servers keep caches and `node_modules` in the site's folder, so previews
  mount it read-write, and sites in one preview service can reach each other:
  run one service per group of sites that trust each other.
- A dev server sees `PATH`, `HOME`, public names such as `PUBLIC_*` and
  `VITE_*`, and what `PREVIEW_ENV` lists: never the service's other variables,
  nor the studio's cookies.
- `PREVIEW_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=1` installs with `--ignore-scripts`; a package that
  compiles on install then fails.
- `PREVIEW_MAX_RUNNING` dev servers (six) run at once, the longest unused
  stopping for one more, and a failing one waits longer before each retry.
- A build whose output holds a link pointing outside it is not put live.
- That code can write the folder's `.git/config`, so the studio gives git a copy
  holding only remotes, branches and identity, and refuses to publish while the
  file names anything else. Git LFS, an SSH command or a credential helper go
  in the machine's own config (`git config --global`), which is the operator's
  and is used as it is. A remote that is a folder on the same machine is pushed
  to without its hooks; `greatcms studio` on your own checkout trusts its config.
- It can also write `.git/objects/info/alternates`, which tells git to read
  objects from another repository. The studio runs no git in a folder where
  that file names anything outside it, and says how to undo it
  (`git repack -a -d`, then delete the file).

## Declaring sites up front

Sites are usually connected in the studio. A server can also come up already
managing its sites, under ids that do not change between restarts, because
the id is part of the form address every contact form posts to.
`STUDIO_SITES` does that:

```sh
STUDIO_SITES='[{"id":"my-site","path":"/srv/sites/my-site","devUrl":"https://preview.example.com","deployRoot":"/srv/www","pushAfterPublish":false}]'
```

`deployRoot` is the builder's `DEPLOY_ROOT` as the studio sees it; mount the
same volume into both. With it, the site page shows what is live, a build that
failed with its log, and the releases kept on disk. **Put this back live**
asks the builder to swap to one of them by writing its commit into a
`rollback` file there; the studio still runs nothing of the site's. The
rolled-back release stays live until the next publish, which goes out as usual.

On start the studio adds any site it does not have and brings the rest in line
with the list. An id that already points at a different folder is refused
rather than silently moved.

## Images

Both servers are published as images on every release, so a server needs no
GreatCMS checkout:

```
ghcr.io/uwenayoallain/greatcms-studio
ghcr.io/uwenayoallain/greatcms-deploy      # also runs greatcms-preview
```

The studio's is Alpine, Node, git and one bundled file. The builder's is
Debian, for the native packages sites install.

## Sharing the preview

The link icon above the editor's preview makes a link anyone can open for
seven days, unpublished edits included, without a studio account. It works
through the same `forward_auth` check: the link carries a signed token, the
studio trades it for a cookie that opens that site's preview and nothing else.
**Stop sharing**, on the link's page and in site settings, ends that site's
links; changing `STUDIO_PASSWORD` ends every site's.

## Live preview on the server

The editor frames the site's dev server beside the form, so a change is seen
rendered before it is published. On a server that means running the dev server
there too, in the same working copy the studio writes drafts into, and it must
not be open to the world.

The studio vouches for it. `GET /auth/check` answers `204` when the request
carries a signed-in session and otherwise redirects to the studio's sign-in,
which comes back to the page that was wanted. Caddy's `forward_auth` asks it
before every preview request:

```
preview.example.com {
	forward_auth studio:8787 {
		uri /auth/check
	}
	reverse_proxy preview:4321
}
```

The studio's own session cookie never leaves the studio's host, because the
preview runs the site's code and would otherwise receive it; over HTTPS it is
named `__Host-greatcms_session`, a name a preview cannot set. Signing in also
sets a second cookie for the parent domain that opens the preview and nothing
else. For that, the studio has to know the domain and its own address:

| Variable               | Meaning                                                        |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `STUDIO_URL`           | Where browsers reach the studio, `https://studio.example.com`. |
| `STUDIO_COOKIE_DOMAIN` | The parent domain, `example.com`. Unset: this host only.       |

Use both only over HTTPS. Over plain http no cookie can be tied to the
studio's own host, so a preview under the same domain could set cookies the
studio reads: the studio prints a warning at start and runs all the same.

A redirect is only ever issued to a host under that domain. With both set, an
editor who is signed in to the studio sees the preview, in the frame and in a
tab, and nobody else does. There is no second password. The dev server itself
has to accept the name it is reached by; the example passes `PREVIEW_HOST` to
Astro's `vite.server.allowedHosts`.

The preview is optional: without it the editor still publishes, and the
builder shows the result a few seconds later.

The studio says when a dev server is not running: on the sites list, on the
site's page, and over the editor's preview, instead of framing an error page.
It checks by connecting to the dev server, so it needs an address it can reach
itself. When browsers reach the preview somewhere else, through the proxy
above, give the site a `probeUrl` in `STUDIO_SITES` naming the dev server
directly, such as `"probeUrl":"http://preview:4321"`.

### Only while someone is editing

A dev server is the one heavy process in the stack, and it is only useful
while an editor is looking. `greatcms-preview`, in the same package and image
as the builder, stands where the dev server would: the first request starts
it, every request keeps it alive, and after `PREVIEW_IDLE` seconds of silence
(fifteen minutes by default) it is stopped. While it comes up the browser gets
a small page that asks again every two seconds, so the editor's frame fills in
by itself.

| Variable          | Meaning                                                               |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PREVIEW_SOURCE`  | The site's working copy, the same folder the studio writes drafts to. |
| `PREVIEW_COMMAND` | Starts the dev server on `$PORT`; default installs and runs Astro.    |
| `PREVIEW_IDLE`    | Seconds without a request before it is stopped.                       |

`GET /__greatcms/preview` reports whether it is stopped, starting or running.
Reloads pass through the same proxy, WebSockets included, so a draft still
shows as you type.

### Every site from one service

For many sites, run one `greatcms-preview` with `PREVIEW_SITES` naming the
list the studio writes to `STUDIO_PREVIEWS_FILE`. With
`STUDIO_PREVIEW_URL=https://{site}-preview.example.com`, a site connected
without a dev URL gets the next free name, and the service routes by host, so
one `*.example.com` block proxying to it covers every site.
`STUDIO_PREVIEW_PROBE` is where the studio checks the service is up.

Each dev server comes from the site's `package.json` (Astro, Next.js, Nuxt,
SvelteKit, Vite, or a `dev` script), installed first if needed.

## Behind a Cloudflare Tunnel

A studio on a machine with no public address, or with no ports you want open,
can be reached through a Cloudflare Tunnel instead of a reverse proxy.
`apps/studio/tunnel/` runs the studio beside `cloudflared`, and the studio's
port is never published, so the tunnel is the only way in:

```sh
cd apps/studio/tunnel
cp .env.example .env    # the tunnel token, STUDIO_HOST, a password, the sites
docker compose up -d --build
```

Create the tunnel in Cloudflare and give it one public hostname,
`studio.example.com`, pointing at `http://studio:8787`. Cloudflare terminates
TLS and tells the studio so, which keeps its cookies `Secure`; the compose file
sets `STUDIO_TRUST_PROXY=cloudflare`, so rate limiting sees each visitor's own
address. `SITES_DIR` is mounted at the same path inside the container, so the
paths in `STUDIO_SITES` are the ones on the host.

The preview a site's `devUrl` names is framed by the editor's browser, not by
the server, so a `localhost` address works only on the machine running the dev
server. The same compose file also runs the previews for editors anywhere:

- `previews` is the preview service above, serving every connected site's dev
  server inside the compose network only. It sets `GREATCMS_PREVIEW_SERVER=1`,
  so the Astro integration and the Nuxt module leave out the framework's dev
  toolbar, which costs round trips over a remote link.
- `caddy` sits in front of it and asks the studio's `/auth/check` about each
  visitor, so a preview opens for someone signed in to the studio and for
  nobody else.
- Set `PREVIEW_DOMAIN=example.com`, and a site connected from folder `my-site`
  previews at `my-site-preview.example.com`. Give the tunnel one wildcard
  hostname, `*.example.com` to `http://caddy:80`, after the studio's (or one
  hostname per preview, if other names must not reach the tunnel).

`SITES_DIR` is the sites folder the connect page lists and clones into;
`SITES_ROOT` names another when `SITES_DIR` is a single repository. Signing in
sets the preview cookie for `PREVIEW_DOMAIN` too, and it opens the previews
and nothing else.

### Bring your own domain

Anyone can run a studio of their own on their own domain, with this tunnel or
the server stack below. A studio hosts only the sites its owner connects:
signing in, with GitHub or a password, never adds one.

## A complete example

`examples/studio-astro/deploy/` holds a `compose.yaml` and `Caddyfile` that
run all of this on one machine from one setting. `DOMAIN=example.com` in
`.env` gives the site at the apex and `www`, the studio at `studio.example.com`
and the preview at `preview.example.com`, with Caddy on 80 and 443 fetching
certificates for all four. Clone the site into `/srv/sites`, point the four
DNS records at the server, and `COMPOSE_BAKE=false docker compose up -d --build`
(the images build on the host network, which the bake builder refuses). The same files
with `compose.local.yaml` run everything on `localhost` ports first; browsers
share cookies across ports, so the sign-in covers the preview there too.


---
title: Previewing
source: apps/docs/content/docs/previewing.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/previewing
---

# Previewing

> Your own dev server renders it. Never the studio.

## In your own dev server

Point a local site at your dev server's URL and the editor shows your real
components beside the form. Publishing writes the files, your dev server
reloads, and the pane updates: usually within a couple of seconds.

It takes one dev-only line in your framework's config, and `greatcms init`
adds it for you:

| Framework        | One line                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Astro            | `astro.config`: `integrations: [greatcms()]` from `@greatcms/reader/astro`                                   |
| Next.js          | root layout: `<GreatcmsPreview />` inside `<head>`, from `@greatcms/reader/next`                             |
| Nuxt             | `nuxt.config`: `modules: ["@greatcms/reader/nuxt"]`                                                          |
| SvelteKit        | `vite.config`: `greatcmsWatch()` and `src/hooks.server`: `greatcmsHandle`, from `@greatcms/reader/sveltekit` |
| Other Vite sites | `vite.config`: `plugins: [greatcmsWatch()]` from `@greatcms/reader/vite`                                     |

The reader reads content with the filesystem, which is what keeps it
framework-neutral, and it also means a dev server has no idea those files are
dependencies. The Vite-based integrations watch them and reload the page.
`next dev` cannot be told about them, so the Next.js component asks the studio
to reload the frame after each edit instead.

Everything here runs only in development and only while the studio frames the
page. A built page carries none of it, and on your own tab nothing changes.

## As you type, in your own site

Connect a site as a folder on this machine, give it your dev server's URL, and
the editor shows that dev server beside the form. Each edit is written to
`.cms/draft/` in your working copy; your dev server notices and reloads, so your
own components render content nobody has published.

There is no approximation of your design, because there is no approximation: it
is your site. Publishing writes the real content file and clears the draft.

Three rules keep drafts safe. The reader only reads them when `NODE_ENV` is
`development`, so a build can never render one. `.cms/draft/` ignores itself, so
one can never be committed. And publishing clears the draft it came from, so the
site stops showing an edit that has already landed.

Without JavaScript nothing is written as you type, and the editor still
publishes: the frame simply shows the site as last published.

## Pointing at the page

The framed page knows what the form holds. Switch on **Select** above the
preview and the page is dissected: move over it and the heading, paragraph,
image or section under the pointer is outlined with its field's name; click,
and that field opens and takes focus in the form. **Sections** outlines every
block on the page at once, so a long page reads as the list of sections it is.
It runs the other way too: land in a field in the form and the page scrolls to
where it renders. The header and footer belong to site regions rather than to
the page, and they are on the page all the same: click the footer while editing
a page and the Footer editor opens at the field you clicked.

No markup is needed for this. The inspector matches each field's value to what
the page shows, which covers headings, copy, rich text and images. Where a site
transforms a value before printing it, or shows the same words twice, two
attributes make the match explicit:

```html
<h2 data-greatcms-field="blocks.0.title">{title}</h2>
<section data-greatcms-block="block-0">…</section>
```

The field path is the one the form uses, dotted; a block's id is `block-` and
its position. Both are plain attributes, so a built page keeps them and nothing
reads them there.

The inspector is part of the script the dev server injects while the page is
framed, so a visitor never downloads it and the studio never reaches into your
page: the two sides talk only through messages, each checking the other is
who framed it. It draws its outlines in a shadow root on an inert,
`aria-hidden` element, so your CSS cannot restyle them and screen readers never
meet them. It changes nothing on `<html>`, which React and Vue would report as
a hydration mismatch, and it survives client-side navigation, Astro's view
transitions included. Clicks belong to the page except while **Select** is on.

## Opening the page being edited

By default the frame opens the front of the site. Tell the studio where each
collection's entries live and it opens the page you are editing instead:

```yaml
# .cms/config.yaml
preview:
  paths:
    pages: { home: "/", "*": "/{slug}" }
    updates: "/updates/{slug}"
```

A plain path with `{slug}` covers most collections; a map lets one slug be the
front page. Regions, which are part of every page, preview at `/`.

## Getting rid of an unsaved edit

Leave the editor and come back and the draft is still in the form, with a
notice saying so: the preview and the form always show the same thing, and
publishing publishes what you see. "Discard unsaved edits" beside the frame
throws the draft away and puts your dev server back to what is published. It
is a plain form post, so it works with JavaScript switched off.

Anything still unsaved is listed on the site's page in the studio, and
`npx greatcms doctor` names it from the terminal: a draft you forgot is
otherwise visible only in dev, which is exactly where you would stop noticing
it.

For a dev server with none of the integrations above, **Reload the site**
beside the frame reloads it by hand.

## Pages built from a collection

Astro's dev server caches what `getStaticPaths()` returns. If it passes each
entry to the page as a prop, the preview keeps showing that cached copy and
never your edit. Return only the slug, and read the entry in the page itself:

```astro
---
export function getStaticPaths() {
  return cms.collection("pages").map((page) => ({ params: { slug: page.slug } }));
}

const page = cms.collection("pages").find((entry) => entry.slug === Astro.params.slug);
---
```

A build reads each entry once either way, so this costs nothing in production.

## The studio never builds your site

The studio cannot render a Hugo site, or a Laravel one, so it does not pretend
to. Building your site inside the studio would also break the rule that it never
executes anything from a repository it manages. Your dev server renders the
preview, on your machine, with your toolchain; your CI builds what you publish.


---
title: Forms and submissions
source: apps/docs/content/docs/forms-and-submissions.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/forms-and-submissions
---

# Forms and submissions

> The one thing Git cannot hold, collected in one inbox.

Git cannot hold a message someone typed on your site. The studio takes it
directly, so there is no third-party form service and no per-site backend to
provision.

```html
<form method="POST" action="https://your-studio/f/{siteId}/contact">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required />

  <input type="hidden" name="_redirect" value="/thanks/" />
  <input type="hidden" name="_t" value="1755024000000" />

  <button>Send</button>
</form>
```

No JavaScript is involved. Adding a site to the inbox is a row in a table.

## Reserved fields

| Field       | Meaning                                                     |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `_redirect` | Where to send the visitor afterwards. Same-site paths only. |
| `_t`        | When the form was rendered, in epoch milliseconds.          |
| `company`   | Honeypot. Hide it visually _and_ from assistive technology. |

## Spam

Scored from the honeypot, the gap between render and submit, and link density:
never a CAPTCHA, which taxes every legitimate visitor to inconvenience a bot
that solves them anyway. Suspected spam is stored and hidden rather than
discarded, so nothing is lost silently.

## Limits

Each visitor address may submit 20 times a minute. Each site stores at most
1,000 submissions a day and sends at most 60 notification emails an
hour, however many addresses the traffic comes from. Past the email limit,
submissions are still stored; they just stop arriving in your mailbox until the
hour turns over.

Submissions across every site land in one inbox, with read state, CSV export,
and optional email notification.


---
title: Accessibility
source: apps/docs/content/docs/accessibility.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/accessibility
---

# Accessibility

> What is enforced by the format, and what is enforced by tests.

Accessibility here is structural where it can be, and a test where it cannot.

## Enforced by the format

`alt` is required on every image field by default. A field may declare
`alt: decorative-allowed`, which is the only way an empty alt validates: making
an inaccessible image a deliberate authoring act rather than an oversight.
Invalid content is refused before it reaches your repository.

Image width and height are read from the uploaded file's own header and stored
alongside it, so pages do not reflow while images load.

## Enforced by tests

The studio ships **zero JavaScript**. Every screen is server-rendered and every
mutation is a form POST: including adding, removing, and reordering blocks in a
block list. That is what makes the editor keyboard-operable and
screen-reader-legible by construction, rather than by patching ARIA onto
hand-built widgets.

axe runs against every studio screen and every page of the example site on each
CI run, with zero violations allowed. Errors are attached with `aria-invalid`
and `aria-describedby` rather than colour alone. The example site carries a
weight budget so "fast" cannot quietly stop being true.


---
title: Any language
source: apps/docs/content/docs/any-language.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/any-language
---

# Any language

> The standard is files. A reader in Python passes the same suite as the one in TypeScript.

A site is managed by GreatCMS if it contains a schema file and reads content
from the paths the standard describes. That is the entire integration surface.
Hugo, Laravel, or a hand-rolled Go generator consume it exactly as
Astro does, because none of them need anything but YAML and JSON.

The JavaScript packages are a convenience, not a requirement.

## What a reader has to get right

Four cases, all of them in the conformance fixtures because naive
implementations get them wrong:

- **A region with no content file.** It resolves to the schema's `default`
  values. It is not an error.
- **Content written before a field was added.** The new field takes its default;
  the stored fields are kept.
- **A block missing a defaulted field.** Each block in a list is merged over its
  own block type's defaults.
- **A decorative image with empty alt text.** Valid only when the field is
  marked `alt: decorative-allowed`.

The rules are in [section 6 of the standard](/spec/#6-resolution-rules-the-important-part):
objects merge deeply, arrays are replaced wholesale, and a missing schema is a
loud error where a missing content file is not.

## Proving it

```sh
npx @greatcms/conformance fixtures        # prints the path to the fixture site
python3 read.py "$(npx @greatcms/conformance fixtures)" ./out
npx @greatcms/conformance verify ./out
# conformance: PASS
```

Point your reader at the fixture site, write every resolved region to
`<region-id>.json`, and, if it implements collections,
`entries/<collection>/<slug>.json`. The verifier compares each against the
expected document and reports collections separately, so a regions-only reader
still gets a useful answer.

## The reference in Python

`examples/reader-python/read.py` is a complete reader in about 120 lines of
Python, standard library plus PyYAML, written from the standard alone. CI runs
it against the fixtures on every build. It exists to keep the project honest:
if integrating in a new language needs more than one file's worth of code, the
standard has drifted towards whatever is convenient for JavaScript, and that is
a bug.

One detail it has to handle: the standard reads YAML 1.2, where `no` and `off`
are strings and a date is a string. PyYAML implements 1.1, so the reader
replaces the implicit type resolvers rather than patching the results.

## The machine-readable surface

The schemas for both `.cms` files are published as JSON Schema, which is what
gives editors autocomplete and lets a tool in any language validate a schema
before reading content:

- [/json-schema/schema.schema.json](/json-schema/schema.schema.json)
- [/json-schema/config.schema.json](/json-schema/config.schema.json)

For agents, [/llms.txt](/llms.txt) indexes every page, [/llms-full.txt](/llms-full.txt)
holds them in one fetch, and [/docs.json](/docs.json) lists the integration
steps. Every page here is also served as Markdown at its own path plus `.md`.


---
title: For coding agents
source: apps/docs/content/docs/for-agents.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/for-agents
---

# For coding agents

> Every surface an agent needs to wire a site up unattended, and the skill that teaches it.

"Integrate from the standard in half an hour" should hold for a coding agent as
much as for a person. These are the surfaces, each reachable in one fetch, each
generated from the same sources as the pages people read, so they cannot
drift.

| Surface                              | Address                                    |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Index and integration summary        | `/llms.txt`                                |
| Every document in one file           | `/llms-full.txt`                           |
| Each page as Markdown                | `/spec.md`, `/docs/<page>.md`, `/index.md` |
| Manifest with entry points and steps | `/docs.json`                               |
| JSON Schema for `.cms/schema.yaml`   | `/json-schema/schema.schema.json`          |
| JSON Schema for `.cms/config.yaml`   | `/json-schema/config.schema.json`          |

## The skill

The repository ships an agent skill, `skills/greatcms/SKILL.md`: the commands,
the file shapes, the pitfalls and the checks, written to be followed without a
person in the loop. Install it into Claude Code, Cursor or any agent that
reads the open skills format:

```sh
npx skills add uwenayoallain/thegreatcms@greatcms
```

## In the repository

`greatcms init` leaves a section in the site's `AGENTS.md` between
`<!-- greatcms:start -->` and `<!-- greatcms:end -->`, saying where content
lives, what to run before committing, and what not to touch. Running `init`
again updates that section and leaves the rest of the file alone.

Two commands produce machine-readable output for an agent to act on:

```sh
npx greatcms check --json     # every content file against the schema; exit code for CI
npx greatcms doctor --json    # regions, collections, what is still at defaults, unsaved drafts
npx greatcms describe         # every field you may write, its type and limits, and where its file goes
```

Errors from every command carry their remedy on a `fix:` line, in the exact
text that reaches stderr, so an agent can apply it rather than guess.

## What an agent should never do

Call the studio from a page, write into `.cms/draft/`, or ship JavaScript from
GreatCMS to a public site. The [invariants](/docs/the-hybrid-model/) are the
same for agents as for people.


---
title: The examples
source: apps/docs/content/docs/examples.md
url: https://greatcms.uwe.rw/docs/examples
---

# The examples

> Six sites on Astro, Next.js, SvelteKit and Nuxt, and a Python reader, each built to prove one thing.

Every example in the repository is also a test. They build in CI, run axe with
zero violations allowed, and assert that their output contains no script tag.

## A minimal site

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-site-astro dev     # http://localhost:4321
```

`examples/site-astro` is the smallest honest demonstration. The home page puts a
managed hero next to a hand-written section, and both end up in the same static
HTML. A managed block list holds features and pull quotes an editor can
reorder. A blog collection is Markdown with frontmatter, which is what every
static site generator already expects. A contact form posts straight to the
studio with no JavaScript.

The about page is the interesting one: there is no `about.intro.json` in the
repository, so it renders the defaults declared in the schema. The page was
correct before the studio had ever been opened.

## A studio site with real motion

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-studio-astro dev
```

`examples/studio-astro` is Paraline, a fictional design and motion studio, and
the showcase: the kind of site people assume needs a heavyweight CMS and a
JavaScript framework. Every word on it is managed: a studio identity, a hero
whose headline lines and rotating words are lists, a home page of reorderable
sections (client strip, selected work with two variants, a statement, services,
a process, numbers, a quote, a call to action), a contact page, and a JSON
collection of case studies whose covers are generated from a palette and a
motif chosen in the editor.

The motion is the site's own. Scroll-driven CSS does the reading-along
statement, the stacked services, the pinned sideways process, the counting
numbers and the case-study covers that morph into their page through
cross-document view transitions. A small script (under 8 KB compressed, using
Motion) adds what CSS cannot know, such as where the pointer is, and stands in
for scroll timelines where a browser lacks them. Everything stops for visitors
who ask for less motion, and the tests check that no animation starts outside
that preference.

`deploy/` beside it is the complete self-hosted stack for a site like this.

## A ceramics studio, made the way you would make yours

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-ceramics-astro dev
```

`examples/ceramics-astro` is Ibumba, a pottery studio in Kigali that sells its
work and teaches classes. It began as `npm create astro` and `greatcms init`,
the path a new site takes, so it shows what that produces once someone designs
it. A home page of reorderable sections (a statement on two backgrounds, the
steps from clay to kiln, the next few workshops, a quote), a visiting page with
opening hours, and a `workshops` collection whose entries carry a date and
time, a level, a price in Rwandan francs and a fully-booked switch that hides
the booking. The booking form posts to the studio's inbox.

Times are stored with their offset and shown in Kigali's zone, so a build on a
server in another zone prints the same hour. `preview.paths` names the page
each region lives on, so editing the visiting hours frames `/visit/`, not the
front page. No page ships a script.

## A bakery on Next.js

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-bakery-next dev
```

`examples/bakery-next` is Hearth, a neighbourhood bakery, on Next.js 16 with
the App Router. Server Components call the reader in `lib/cms.ts`, so content
is read on the server while the page renders and never reaches the browser as
a request. `output: "export"` writes every page as HTML, so any static host,
or `greatcms-deploy`, serves the folder as it is. The site has a notice bar an
editor can switch on for a holiday, opening hours as a list of groups, and a
`menu` collection with categories, prices and dietary tags, set like a printed
card. The pre-order form is a checkbox group that posts to the studio's inbox,
which keeps every box that was ticked.

`next dev` renders on every request, so the studio's drafts appear on the next
load. It does not watch content files, so `<GreatcmsPreview />` in the root
layout tells the studio, which reloads the preview after each draft. The
preview script is added only under `next dev`. No page has a client
component, so a step after `next build` removes the Next.js runtime from the
export, about 450 KB a visitor had no use for, and fails the build if a page
ever needs it. The tests check that an exported page runs no script and stays
under 50 KB with everything it loads.

## A journal on SvelteKit

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-journal-sveltekit dev
```

`examples/journal-sveltekit` is The Long Light, a writer's essays: a Markdown
collection with a date, a dek and tags, set in Newsreader and prerendered as
plain HTML. `csr = false` keeps SvelteKit's runtime off every page, the 404 is
a real prerendered route rather than the SPA fallback, and the reader's Vite
plugin reloads the page as the studio writes drafts. Its newsletter region has
no content file at all and renders the schema's defaults.

## A product changelog on Nuxt

```sh
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-changelog-nuxt dev
```

`examples/changelog-nuxt` is Sundial, a product landing page and changelog on
Nuxt 4. A Nitro server route calls the reader in `server/api/cms.get.ts`, and
`nuxt generate` writes every page as static HTML with `noScripts: true` on
production routes so no client bundle ships. Releases are Markdown files with a
version, date and kind, and the beta waitlist form posts straight to the
studio's inbox.

## This site

`apps/docs` is the website you are reading. The landing page's headline, the
claims, and the closing note are JSON in the repository, edited in the studio.
The layout around them is ordinary Astro. The standard page renders `SPEC.md`
directly, so the published document and the one the code implements cannot
drift, and the docs pages are a Markdown collection like any blog.

## A reader in Python

`examples/reader-python/read.py` reads the standard without any of the
JavaScript packages and passes the conformance suite. See
[Any language](/docs/any-language/).

## Running any of them from the studio

Start the studio, add the example's folder as a site, and give it the dev
server's URL. Edits appear in your own dev server as you type, and publishing
commits to this repository like it would to yours.
